title: The Global Hum: Scientists Close In on the Source of a Mystery Sound
summary:
It's a sound that has haunted people for nearly 50 years: a deep, droning hum that seems to come from nowhere and everywhere at once. Known simply as 'The Hum,' this low-frequency noise is heard by an estimated 2 to 4 percent of the global population. For some, it's a minor irritation. For others, it causes physical discomfort, nausea, and a sensation of vibration passing through the body. The hum is most noticeable indoors and at night, yet often only certain people in a room can perceive it.

The phenomenon first gained widespread attention in Bristol, England, in the mid-1970s, when the local newspaper received a flood of letters from perplexed residents. Initial theories pointed to industrial fans, but the reports persisted long after the suspected warehouse closed. Since then, the hum has been documented in the United States—starting in Taos, New Mexico, and Kokomo, Indiana—as well as in Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and across Europe. Canadian teacher Glen MacPherson, after experiencing the hum himself, launched the World Hum Map and Database Project in 2012 to collect reports and map the phenomenon.

Explanations have ranged from the mundane to the outlandish: ventilation systems, heat pumps, wind turbines, ocean waves, and even conspiracy theories involving secret government projects or aliens. Now, researchers at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) are taking a rigorous scientific approach. Professor Markus Drexl and his team examined 28 individuals in Germany who report hearing the hum. They tested two core hypotheses: first, that the hum originates from an external low-frequency sound source; second, that it stems from an internal physiological mechanism, such as spontaneous otoacoustic emissions—sounds generated by the inner ear itself.

The study used precise audiological measurements to see how the subjects' ears and brains responded to low-frequency tones. While the full results are still being analyzed, this work represents a crucial step toward distinguishing between environmental and biological causes. If the hum is external, mitigation strategies like soundproofing could help. If it's internal, treatments might target the auditory system directly. For the millions who hear the maddening hum, a definitive answer can't come soon enough.
why_it_matters: The hum mystery matters because it shows how even common experiences can go unexplained, highlighting the need for science to take unusual but widespread health complaints seriously. Finding the cause could also improve how we design quiet spaces and understand our own hearing.

background_read: In the mid-1970s, residents of Bristol, England (a large city in southwest England) began writing to newspapers about a strange, persistent drone. Despite a nearby warehouse closing its industrial fans, the hum continued, marking the start of the modern phenomenon.

Similar reports later emerged in the United States—most famously in Taos, New Mexico, and Kokomo, Indiana—and in many other countries. Glen MacPherson, a Canadian teacher who hears the hum himself, launched the World Hum Map and Database Project in 2012 to track global reports and look for patterns.

Scientists at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU, a leading research university in Trondheim, Norway) are now investigating using precise hearing tests. The idea that the hum might come from the inner ear is based on 'spontaneous otoacoustic emissions'—faint sounds that healthy ears actually produce, discovered by researchers in the 1970s.

Low-frequency noise, like the hum, travels much farther through the ground and buildings than higher-pitched sounds, which makes it extremely difficult to locate its source. Some external suspects include industrial equipment, gas pipelines, and even ocean waves crashing on distant shores.

perspectives.description: Sufferers may finally get relief if science identifies the cause, whether environmental or biological. Communities like Bristol and Taos could see renewed trust in experts who long dismissed their complaints.

Living with an unexplained, intrusive noise causes real distress, and past dismissals have left hum hearers feeling isolated. Some worry that the study could fail to find a clear answer, prolonging the misery for millions.

The Hum sits at the intersection of environmental noise pollution, psychology, and inner-ear biology. Systematically separating external and internal factors is a classic scientific challenge that will require ruling out many variables, from industrial machinery to ocean waves.

If otoacoustic emissions prove to be the culprit, new therapies or devices might help mask or reduce perception. If external, improved urban planning and noise regulation could mitigate similar issues and help quiet the world for everyone.
